name: Containers
summary: Your app and everything it needs, packed into one portable image.
howItWorks: A container image bundles your code with its runtime, libraries and config. When it runs, the host’s kernel isolates it into its own processes, filesystem and network. Containers share the host’s kernel instead of booting their own, so they start in seconds and use a fraction of the memory a VM needs, letting one machine run many of them.
analogy: A shipping container. The crane, the ship and the truck don’t care what’s inside, because the box is always the same shape.
useWhen: Ending “works on my machine”: dev, CI and production run the same image
Packaging services that need specific library versions
Running many small services densely on shared machines
avoidWhen: Apps that need a different kernel or a desktop GUI
A tiny task triggered a few times a day, where a serverless function is simpler
example: A data team ships a Python API as `api:1.4.2`. The same image runs on a developer’s laptop, in the CI test job and in production. Upgrading means publishing a new tag.

diagram.caption: A Dockerfile becomes one tagged image in a registry. Every environment pulls that exact image, so they all run the same bits.

story: The idea of fencing a program in without giving it a whole machine goes back to 1979, when Version 7 Unix added `chroot`, which changes the directory a process sees as the root of the filesystem. It only hid files, though. Hosting companies wanted more: FreeBSD’s jails, released in FreeBSD 4.0 in March 2000, were sponsored by a web hosting company and aimed at providers that needed to keep their own services apart from their customers’, and they also restricted networking and visibility of other processes.

Linux built containers from separate pieces. Namespaces, starting with mount namespaces in 2002, gave a process its own view of mounts, process IDs, networks and users. In 2006 Google engineers Paul Menage and Rohit Seth started “process containers” to limit the CPU and memory a group of processes could use; renamed control groups, it was merged into Linux 2.6.24 in January 2008. LXC combined both that year.

The pieces were powerful but awkward until Docker (2013) wrapped them in a simple tool and a portable image format. The Open Container Initiative standardised that format and runtime in 2015, and orchestrators such as Kubernetes made them a mainstream way to run server software.

choices.why: Programs use the normal system call interface with nothing emulated, so a container starts as fast as a process and costs little memory. The price is that every container must run on the host’s kind of kernel, and they all trust it.

choices.choice: Partition the system instead of adding fine-grained permissions
choices.why: FreeBSD’s jail designers kept Unix’s simple all-powerful root, but confined each root to its own slice of the system. Delegating a whole environment proved easier than writing detailed access rules.

choices.choice: Isolation assembled from separate kernel features
choices.why: Linux added namespaces (what a process can see) and cgroups (what it can use) independently over years. That made them flexible but fiddly, which is why tools like LXC and Docker exist to combine them.

choices.choice: Ship the whole filesystem as an image
choices.why: Isolation alone didn’t solve shipping software. Docker packaged the app and its libraries into a portable, layered image, which turned containers into a way to deploy software as well as a sandbox.

timeline.text: FreeBSD 4.0 ships jails for shared hosting
Linux 2.4.19 adds mount namespaces, the first namespace
cgroups merged into Linux 2.6.24; LXC released
Docker launches; Linux user namespaces enable unprivileged containers
Open Container Initiative formed to standardise images and runtimes
Kubernetes 1.24 removes its built-in Docker support
